articles.title: Zoe Stratford gives birth to baby girl - a year after England World Cup triumph
articles.summary: Zoe Stratford, who captained England to World Cup glory a year ago, gives birth to a baby girl.
articles.body:
England's World Cup-winning captain Zoe Stratford has given birth to her first child.

Stratford - nee Aldcroft - gave birth to a baby girl, who is currently nameless, on Wednesday.

England beat Canada in the World Cup final in September 2025.

Stratford, 29, joined Sale Sharks from Gloucester-Hartpury in the summer, having played a key role in their rise to become the dominant force in the women's domestic game.

Commenting on an Instagram , external post announcing the birth by Stratford's husband Luke, Sale said: "The most amazing news!"

Stratford was named World Player of the Year in 2021 and co-captained Gloucester-Hartpury to three back-to-back Premiership Women's Rugby titles.

She was the third England women's player to announce she was expecting this year, following Bristol's Lark Atkin-Davies and Abbie Ward.

In April England team-mates Marlie Packer and Rosie Galligan announced they are expecting a baby together, with lock Galligan due to give birth this month.

Meg Jones, who was named England captain after Stratford's pregnancy announcement, has recently called for England players to have access to fertility support and egg freezing.

images.caption: Image caption, Zoe Stratford has won 69 Test caps since making her England debut in 2016

articles.title: Ireland v Japan: Jane Clohessy and Niamh Gallagher to make first starts
articles.summary: Ireland head coach Scott Bemand hands first starts to Jane Clohessy and Niamh Gallagher for Saturday's Test with Japan.
articles.body:
Ireland head coach Scott Bemand has handed first starts to Jane Clohessy and Niamh Gallagher for Saturday's Test with Japan.

The trio of Sophie Barrett, Kate Jordan and Alana McInerney are set to make their Ireland debuts off the bench.

Ireland defeated Japan in the WXV Global Series in Galway on Sunday and the sides will face off again in a Test at Virgin Media Park in Cork.

Bemand's side are back in WXV action with a double-header with South Africa later in October.

Munster's Clohessy will win her third cap with a maiden start in the second row, while full-back Gallagher has been named in the starting team for the first time.

Despite the chance to offer new faces experience, there are also plenty of experienced names in Bemand's line-up.

Linda Djougang, Neve Jones and Eilis Cahill make up the front row, with Clohessy and Fiona Tuite-O'Sullivan in the second row.

Erin King captains the side from flanker, and she is joined in the back row by Brittany Hogan and Jemima Adams Verling.

Emily Lane and Dannah O'Brien retain their half-back partnership, while Anna McGann, who has won the majority of her 19 Ireland caps on the wing, will partner Aoife Dalton at centre.

The back three is made up of Beibhinn Parsons and Robyn O'Connor, who join Gallagher on her first start.

Key back row Aoife Wafer will not be risked in the Test after a "minor" training injury kept her out of the team to face Japan last Sunday.

Ireland: Niamh Gallagher; Beibhinn Parsons; Anna McGann, Aoife Dalton; Robyn O'Connor; Dannah O'Brien, Emily Lane; Linda Djougang, Neve Jones, Eilis Cahill; Jane Clohessy, Fiona Tuite-O'Sullivan; Brittany Hogan, Erin King, Jemima Adams Verling.

Replacements: Beth Buttimer, Sadhbh McGrath, Sophie Barrett, Kate Jordan, Grace Moore, Aoibheann Reilly, Enya Breen, Alana McInerney.

images.caption: Image caption, Munster second row Jane Clohessy and full-back Niamh Gallagher have been handed their first Ireland starts against Japan

articles.title: Rugby World Cup 2027: Wales preparations outlined a year out from Australia
articles.summary: With one year to go before the 2027 Rugby World Cup, what lies in wait for Steve Tandy's Wales over the next 12 months before they head to Australia?
articles.body:
It might be hard to believe how quickly it comes around, but Thursday marks a year to go until the men's Rugby World Cup begins in Australia.

The 2027 competition starts on 1 October in Perth with a match between Australia and Hong Kong China, with the tournament finale on 13 November in Sydney.

Wales are to feature in the second game when they open their campaign against Zimbabwe in Adelaide on 2 October.

Steve Tandy's side sit 11th in the world rankings, currently topped by reigning World Cup champions South Africa.

The tournament has expanded from 20 to 24 teams, with the number of pools rising from four to six.

All 12 teams who finished inside the top three of their pools at the 2023 World Cup - France, New Zealand, Italy, Ireland, South Africa, Scotland, Wales, Fiji, Australia, England, Argentina and Japan - qualified automatically.

Georgia, Spain, Romania, Portugal, Tonga, Canada, United States of America, Uruguay, Chile, Zimbabwe, Hong Kong China and Samoa all earned their places through qualifying tournaments.

Wales have 12 or 13 potential matches across three blocks before they travel to Australia.

Nations Championship home matches are set to be staged against Japan, New Zealand and Australia in November, before a final play-off game at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium.

There will be five matches in the 2027 Six Nations, with trips to play France, Scotland and Italy and home fixtures in Cardiff against England and Ireland.

Following the end of the 2026-27 domestic season, Wales will meet up in the summer for fitness camps, with past trips including visits to Poland, Switzerland and Turkey.

There will be three or four World Cup warm-ups in the summer. The Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) has so far refused to publicly announce who they will face next August and September, or even how many games they will play.

The likely scenario is that Wales will play three games in Europe before a warm-up match on the way to or in Australia itself.

Tandy held alignment camps with more than 50 players in September, and the World Cup squad will eventually be whittled down to the final 33.

Wales have been drawn in Pool F alongside England, Tonga and Zimbabwe and will travel to play at three different venues.

The opening game against Zimbabwe will be staged in Adelaide, followed by a six-day turnaround before they face Tonga in Melbourne.

England await eight days later in Sydney on 16 October, before the expanded knockout stages.

Next year's World Cup will feature 16 teams at the knockout phase, rather than the traditional eight who previously went straight to the quarter-finals.

The top two teams from each of the six pools will progress to the last 16 alongside the four best third-place nations.

If Wales were to win their group, they would play the runner-up from pool B, which contains South Africa, Italy, Georgia and Romania.

Should Wales finish second, they would face the second-placed side in pool C, which is made up of Argentina, Fiji, Spain and Canada.

South Africa and New Zealand, World Cup finalists in 2023, are destined to meet in the quarter-finals, set to be staged in Sydney and Brisbane, if they top their groups.

The Olympic Stadium in Sydney will host both semi-finals and the bronze medal match, before staging the showpiece final on Saturday, 13 November.

Saturday, 7 November: Wales v Japan, Principality Stadium, Cardiff, 16:40 GMT

Saturday, 14 November: Wales v New Zealand, Principality Stadium, Cardiff, 14:10 GMT

Saturday, 21 November: Wales v Australia, Principality Stadium, Cardiff, 20:10 GMT

Weekend of November 27-29: Play-off matches, Allianz Stadium, Twickenham

Saturday, 6 February: France v Wales, Stade de France, Paris, 16:40 GMT

Saturday, 13 February: Scotland v Wales, Murrayfield, Edinburgh, 16:40 GMT

Saturday, 20 February: Wales v Ireland, Principality Stadium, Cardiff, 14:10 GMT

Saturday, 6 March: Wales v England, Principality Stadium, Cardiff, 16:40 GMT

Saturday, 13 March: Italy v Wales, Stadio Olimpico, Rome, 14:10 GMT

The Warm Up: One Year To The Rugby World Cup!

Saturday, 2 October: Wales v Zimbabwe, Adelaide Oval, Adelaide, 03:45 BST

Friday, 8 October: Tonga v Wales , Docklands Stadium, Melbourne, 08:15 BST

Saturday, 16 October: England v Wales , Stadium Australia, Sydney, 09:45 BST

Bronze medal match: Saturday, 12 November

Pool A: New Zealand, Australia, Chile, Hong Kong China.

Pool B: South Africa, Italy, Georgia, Romania.

Pool D: Ireland, Scotland, Uruguay, Portugal.

Pool F: England, Wales , Tonga, Zimbabwe.

articles.title: Super League Grand Final: Can you name every team to make the end-of-season finale?
articles.summary: Ahead of Saturday's Super League Grand FInal at Old Trafford, can you name all 11 clubs to make the end-of-season finale since its inception?
articles.body:
The showpiece event in the Super League calendar returns on Saturday as the Grand Final takes place under the lights of Old Trafford.

It has been almost 30 years since the first Grand Final took place at Manchester United's Theatre of Dreams and a fair few faces have taken to the field in that time.

Only five clubs have won the end-of-season finale and just 11 have reached it since its inception.

But can you name every side to reach a Super League Grand Final? Test your knowledge in our quiz below.

Don't forget to share your score with your friends. Good luck!

articles.title: Never played in The Prem, now they face hosts Australia in 2027 World Cup opener
articles.summary: Jack Combes and Alex Post tell BBC Sport about a "dream come true" as they look ahead to the 2027 Rugby World Cup opener against hosts Australia.
articles.body:
It is 1 October 2027. There are 61,000 fans inside Perth Stadium.

There is a global TV audience in the millions as two teams go through their final warm-ups preparing to open the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

For hosts Australia, twice world champions with a proud rugby history across the codes, it is familiar territory.

For their opponents Hong Kong China, it is anything but.

It will be their World Cup debut and for their players it will be biggest match of their lives.

Among them, all being well, are Jack Combes and Alex Post. Two players more used to the lower semi-professional tiers of the English league system than the global spotlight.

It is David v Goliath - in football parlance it is Spain v Cape Verde.

Twelve months earlier to the day, Jack and Alex are in Hong Kong. It is a national holiday and both have taken time out to tell BBC Sport about how their sporting and personal lives have been transformed.

"I think the whole run-up to the whole qualification process was already a dream in itself. To qualify for a men's first World Cup was huge," said Combes, a scrum-half.

There are glints in their eyes and smiles on their faces - why wouldn't there be?

Hong Kong China have been drawn in Pool A at the World Cup, where not just the hosts await, but also Chile - and the All Blacks.

"People will say it's daunting and it's a huge challenge to have those two top nations in your pool, but if you're going to do it, do it properly. Why not?" said Combes.

"People might question whether we deserve to be there. But for me, if you asked anyone as a kid, if you could open up the World Cup in that first game in a year's time, it's genuinely amazing. A dream come true.

"And I'm sure anyone who does give us any criticism about us being there, there's no way they wouldn't be doing the same thing if they could, 100%."

Despite having made his international debut a decade ago, until recently Post was hooking for Richmond in The Champ.

"Unfortunately, I've never played at The Prem level. But The Champ definitely doesn't get the credit it deserves," said the 31-year-old.

"It's a very tough league. And that was great preparation for the international games."

Post was a full-time rugby player with Hong Kong China, before the Covid pandemic brought that to an end and he began a Masters degree at the University of Oxford.

The Varsity match at Twickenham remains one of the larger crowds he has played in front of.

"One of the unique selling points for Hong Kong is the players are contracted all year round and spend all their time together," said Post.

"So it wasn't really feasible for players like myself to stay at Richmond.

"Hong Kong was very much, 'we need boots on the ground'.

"I've moved my family and myself over the last couple of weeks and yeah, kind of chase the dream for the next year."

A full-time professional contract has enabled greater focus on the game away from being a financial analyst.

"With Richmond, we'd train twice a week and then you would do your own gym sessions in your own time," added Post.

"But you can probably do twice as much as that with Hong Kong now."

For Combes, 29, a former student and teacher at Hartpury College, it has been a circuitous route to professional sport that included a spell at Birmingham Moseley in England's third tier.

"So I've been full-time in the sevens for about three and a half years now," he said.

"I've done my career in reverse. I went from teaching after an ACL (anterior cruciate ligament injury), to playing semi-professional rugby, to being a full-time athlete at the age of 25.

"I wouldn't change it for the world, but going into a full-time environment where you have the resources, you have the training time, physical development, it's necessary for what we're facing."

Hong Kong has a proud tradition of rugby stretching back seven decades, not least around its annual sevens tournament.

They qualified for the World Cup by defeating Korea 70-22 in the final round of the Asia Rugby Championship last year.

A late 42-40 victory over fellow World Cup finalists Uruguay in July was perhaps the strongest showing yet of where they stand.

"The mindset's changed from years gone by where you compete in Asia and you play against teams that you know you probably should be beating," said Combes.

"Now we're completely on the other side of the spectrum where we've got nothing to lose.

"I think just be ambitious, be fearless, and go for it.

"'Be memorable' is the phrase that coaches have been talking about."

Both Post and Combes were born in Hong Kong and came up through the age-grade system there. They have witnessed how the game has grown there and are aware of the criticism they have faced, often focused on the international make-up of the team.

"It's always the first criticism we get after an international game," said Post.

"We don't go looking for that criticism or feedback. But it's always going to be there. I think for us, just perform and try and put something out there that people are proud of."

"I was born here in 1997," added Combes.

"Mum is half Chinese and going through the whole minis rugby here where we probably had one of the biggest mini rugby numbers base in the world, up until Covid.

"But I think the game's back growing within local schools - primary, secondary.

"Hopefully we can inspire the next generation."

Former London Irish and Ospreys director of rugby Toby Booth has joined the coaching set-up.

A good test of where they are at will come when Hong Kong China take on three countries in the Nations Cup next month, all with World Cup heritage, in the shape of USA, Canada and Tonga.

"Personally, I've got a whole bunch of pressure just from my family and friends," said Post.

"I've been getting messages all today saying it's one year, you better make the team.

"There will definitely be a big Hong Kong contingent [in Perth]. We want to be everyone's second team."

"You know, we are always going to be the underdogs," said Combes, who is known to his team-mates as Maradona for his keenness to kick any stray footballs that make their way on to the training pitch.

"I think our whole string of games leading into the World Cup with Nations Cup, warm-up games we're always going to be sort of looked over.

"But I think that works in our favour - we're just a bit fearless."

Oh, and remember Spain v Cape Verde at the Fifa World Cup? That ended in a draw.

Image caption, Hong Kong China have been Asia Rugby champions for the past seven years

articles.title: Josh Adams: Wales and Cardiff wing targets third Rugby World Cup
articles.summary: Wales wing Josh Adams is nearing full fitness in time for the autumn internationals and looking forward to a World Cup trip to Australia next year.
articles.body:
Wales wing Josh Adams says he would love to play in a third World Cup as he targets a first trip to Australia next year.

It is exactly a year until Wales play their opening game against Zimbabwe in Adelaide on 2 October, before further pool games against Tonga and England.

"I'm desperate to go, but there is loads of rugby to be played and months ahead of us," said Adams, looking ahead to the tournament.

"It is important that you navigate your way through correctly and get to that start line in a good spot to be selected."

Adams, 31, was the World Cup's top try scorer in the 2019 tournament in Japan with seven as Wales reached the semi-finals.

The Cardiff back, who was also part of the squad that lost a quarter-final to Argentina four years later, insists he is just as excited for a hat-trick of global tournaments.

"I've never been to Australia, so that, as well as playing in a World Cup, is something I'm determined to do," said Adams.

Wales counting down the year until World Cup

The Warm Up: One Year To The Rugby World Cup!

Wales begin the World Cup countdown by playing four matches in the second half of the Nations Championship in November.

Japan, New Zealand and Australia will travel to play in Cardiff before a final play-off match at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.

Adams was ruled out of Wales' 43-0 defeat by South Africa in Durban in July due to a calf injury.

The British and Irish Lions wing has missed Cardiff's start to the season but says he will be fit for international duty next month, with a club return expected in October.

"I am training, but it's important that you navigate your way through correctly and there's no rush," said Adams.

"I had the calf injury in the summer, but I've been good for a while.

"It's making sure that when I'm playing, I'm 100% fit and healthy, and I've had good preparation time."

images.caption: Image caption, Josh Adams has played 72 internationals for Wales

articles.title: Alex Groves' journey from heart surgery to Scarlets
articles.summary: New Scarlets lock Alex Groves describes his remarkable return to rugby following heart surgery.
articles.body:
New Scarlets lock Alex Groves will make his home debut on Saturday when he lines up against the Dragons in the United Rugby Championship (URC).

The fact the 25-year-old is playing at all is remarkable considering he underwent major eight-hour heart surgery in February 2024.

There was not just a question whether he would play again. There was even concern about his survival.

"I was confident as a young boy that I was fit and healthy and never thought anything was wrong with me. It was such a shock when I found out.

"It went very quickly from 'do I need surgery?' to 'am I still going to be playing rugby?' - to 'am I still going be alive in two years' time?'."

Carter and Costelow back for Welsh derby

Scarlets prop Domachowski ruled out for two months

Groves was born and brought up in Johannesburg but, aged 19, moved to join Bristol and would help England Under-20s win a Grand Slam.

As part of Bristol's pre-season preparations in 2021, Groves and his team-mates underwent cardio screenings unavailable to the public without symptoms. After the tests he was informed he had a leaky valve in his heart.

The 6ft 9in (2.06m) lock was told it was nothing abnormal, that one in four people have the issue, and that it would just need to be monitored.

In April 2022 Groves joined Sale Sharks, and during another similar heart screening he was told his situation had deteriorated.

The view of medical experts was that he would need surgery within the next five years to stop his heart from growing to a size where it would not be able to support itself.

On 5 January 2024, Groves' 23rd birthday, he was then told about the discovery of an aneurysm - an abnormal bulge in the wall of a blood vessel - that needed urgent attention.

"I remember they found the problem in August 2023 and from there it was on and off for a couple of months," said Groves.

"I had a test in December and then on my birthday the following year, I went in and saw my surgeon with my parents in Liverpool.

"Thank God my parents were in that meeting with me because I completely shut off and everything my surgeon told me from that point on I did not take in.

“It literally scared the life out of me and I didn't actually retain any information.

"I was on the car ride home back to Manchester and my parents were having to relay all the information.”

He recalled how an initial diagnosis had also been missed because of his unusual height.

"My surgeon said I could not play because they'd found an aneurysm that they'd missed," said Groves.

"That was purely down to the fact MRI machines aren't really built for six foot nine broad-shouldered people.

"I remember getting into that machine and sort of squishing up and by doing that, the extra body mass over my heart meant they missed it.

"But fortunately they found it because one wrong hit to the chest and I would've bled out in a matter of seconds because it was on my aortic artery."

Groves had been planning to play in a Champions Cup match for Sale against Stormers in South Africa in January but had to withdraw.

A month later he was having major surgery. He was on the operating table for eight hours.

"It was terrifying but I think it is more scary for the people closest to you," said Groves.

"I just fell asleep and woke up. But I had my girlfriend at the time and my mum sitting in the waiting room.

Groves said he had been put at ease by the medics before the operation.

"I remember speaking to my anaesthetist who was a big rugby fan," recalled Groves.

"He told me the procedure they were doing was as easy as it is for me as a lock to jump in the line-out.

"It's amazing they're able to do something like that at that level of ease. I thought then I'm going to be fine.

"It's amazing how advanced things have become now.

“If I was a player in my position 10 years ago they probably wouldn't have found the problem.

"Or I would have had to retire or even sadly have passed away.”

Groves spent the next nine months recovering and praised Sale for their part in helping him return to fitness.

The South African-born forward has previously spoken about his lack of motivation during that period, , external and how with different heart rhythms he was sweating and out of breath just climbing up stairs.

"It was a tough rehabilitation process," said Groves.

"Sale Sharks weren't obviously familiar with the process of a patient that has to go through open heart surgery.

Groves was given the all-clear to play again in November 2024 and was loaned out to Championship side Caldy RFC.

He returned to the field in late December in a Championship match against Ealing Trailfinders, 10 months after his surgery.

“Thankfully it was a success,” said Groves.

“I've never had a problem since. It's good as new to be honest.”

Groves left Sale in 2025 and returned to South Africa where he joined the Stormers.

He had a brief period loaned to Scarlets when they went to South Africa, Groves helping the Welsh region solve a lock-injury crisis, starting against Lions and coming off the bench against Sharks.

He joined the Llanelli club permanently for the 2026-27 season and has been embraced by some Scarlets fans his family met in Johannesburg during the Lions game - those supporters are sponsoring Groves during his stay in Wales.

They also helped him with some early accommodation when Groves spent six weeks in a flat above a pub in Llanelli, with the owners helping him settle in.

Groves, who has since moved, made his competitive debut as a replacement in the 21-15 defeat against Cardiff last weekend.

And he is enjoying his time back on the field in a new environment.

"It put things into perspective," said Groves.

"It made me realise how fortunate I am to do what I love and have the family and support I have around me.

"It sort of matured me in a way at a young age. I'm just grateful to be here still doing what I love."

images.caption: Image caption, Alex Groves won the under-20s Grand Slam with England

articles.title: Christian Wade: Newcastle winger close to record in try-dominated Prem
articles.summary: Christian Wade sits four away from Chris Ashton's all-time record of 101 as tries dominate Prem Rugby.
articles.body:
The opening week of the new Prem season was all about tries, tries, tries as the league's 10 teams went on all-out attack.

No fewer than 52 tries were scored across the five matches, setting a record for the opening round of a season, with an average of more than 10 per game and four players claiming hat-tricks as spectators were royally entertained.

Contributing two of those scores was Christian Wade for Newcastle Red Bulls in their 59-26 loss at Northampton Saints, as the veteran winger moves closer to an all-time record.

The 35-year-old is now on 97 career tries in the Prem, only four behind Chris Ashton's record mark of 101.

If Wade stays fit and the Red Bulls continue to play a game where they want to get the ball wide, it's surely only a matter of time before the record is in his hands.

Listen to commentary from BBC Radio Newcastle and BBC Radio Leicester

Wade returned to rugby union last December with Newcastle after a short spell in rugby league with Wigan Warriors and he made no secret of his desire to chase down Ashton's tally .

He only added two last season as the Red Bulls struggled at the bottom, but his two tries on the opening night away to the champions suggest new-look Newcastle are going to be nothing if not entertaining.

It is more than 15 years since Wade scored his first try in Prem Rugby for Wasps but anyone watching his efforts at Franklin's Gardens would not have seen a player of diminishing powers - rather, they would have admired the enduring speed and slipperiness of the Newcastle winger.

"Christian bounces across in front of people where they can't lay a finger on him," Red Bulls head coach Dan McFarland told BBC Sport.

"He can accelerate through a hole and defenders find it very difficult to cope with that."

101 - Chris Ashton (Northampton, Saracens, Sale, Harlequins, Worcester, Leicester)

97 - Christian Wade (Wasps, Gloucester, Newcastle)

92 - Tom Varndell (Leicester, Wasps, Bristol)

72 - Mike Brown (Harlequins, Newcastle, Leicester)

69 - Paul Sackey (Bedford, London Irish, Wasps, Harlequins)

Wade's Prem tries have come for Wasps, Gloucester and now Newcastle across a globetrotting 15-year career.

His sporting journey has also taken in a spell in France with Racing 92 in the Top 14, the 13-man code with Wigan and more than three years in the NFL with the Buffalo Bills, even though he never made it into their main squad.

And that period in America has left an indelible mark, according to his new head coach, as to why Wade remains a feared Prem opponent.

"Christian Wade is a proper professional," said McFarland. "He spent a few years in the NFL and he's clearly taken a lot from that experience in terms of how to look after himself and how to prepare himself as a rugby player.

"He's a really good team man, he's got a lot of time for the young players. He's always calm, a calming and connecting influence.

"Christian's in our leadership group because of his capacity to be able to connect with people. He's a really good person."

Leading Prem try scorers in last five seasons

2025-26: 18 - Tommy Freeman (Northampton), Noah Caluori

2024-25: 13 - Gabriel Ibitoye (Bristol), Ollie Hassell-Collins (Leicester)

2023-24: 14 - Ollie Sleightholme (Northampton)

With Wade four short of equalling Ashton's 101 tally and five tries away from breaking it, the current record holder can feel him coming.

The Slough-born winger is the only player in the top 10 still actively playing, but Ashton believes the mark is eventually going to go a long way past 101 with the type of rugby on offer in the modern Prem.

Last year's top try scorers, Northampton and England's Tommy Freeman and Saracens' teenage starlet Noah Caluori both touched down 18 times, the highest season-ending figure for five years, while Caluori's tally included him scoring five tries per match on two separate occasions against Sale Sharks.

Freeman started this campaign with a hat-trick in the same game as Wade's double and that took his career mark to 58, all at the age of 25.

With the England winger having signed a new contract at Saints and their dynamic games delivering tries by the barrel load, could he be the player to eventually take the record?

"It's happening [the record being broken], but it's not going to last long, whoever takes it," Ashton told BBC's Rugby Union Weekly podcast.

"I think it's going to be absolutely blown to smithereens.

"I sat there on Friday and watched Tommy run in another hat-trick and thought he's going to get 20 this year.

"Give him another five or six years at this rate that we're going, oh my goodness. He's 25 and he's on 58! By the age of 30, he'll have 100 plus.

"Christian Wade is missing more tries per game than he is scoring tries but that probably shows where Newcastle's mindset is."

images.caption: Image caption, Christian Wade's 97 Prem tries are split between three clubs
Image caption, Chris Ashton's swan dive was a regular sight in the English top flight for more than 15 years
Image caption, Tommy Freeman has reached double figures for tries in three of the past five Prem seasons for Northampton

articles.title: Alex Lozowski: Saracens exit was sad and bewildering
articles.summary: Sale centre Alex Lozowski says the end of his decade-long stint at Saracens was an anti-climax after being reduced to a fringe player for his farewell campaign.
articles.body:
Sale centre Alex Lozowski says the end of his decade-long stint at Saracens was "sad" and "bewildering" after being reduced to a fringe player for his farewell campaign.

The 33-year-old England international made only two Prem appearances for Saracens last season, with a 10-minute Champions Cup cameo off the bench his only game time since the end of February.

"It was a sad ending for everyone I suppose," said Lozowski.

"They finished fifth, which is not where they wanted to be, and I wasn't part of it at all.

"It was probably just a bit of a damp squib at the end of the season really, which was a shame. It was bewildering and peculiar to me.

"They have their decisions and their reasons and, even though you can disagree with them as strongly as you like, it doesn't really count for much."

Lozowski, whose form in the 2024-25 season won him call-ups to England's squad for both the autumn internationals and Six Nations, was overlooked in favour of a midfield combination of Olly Hartley and Nick Tomkins for Saracens' run-in.

A streak of five successive victories took the London club to the brink of the play-offs before they lost away to Exeter in a semi-final shootout in the final round of the regular season.

"Sport teaches you all kinds of different lessons and now it's like a distant memory, but at the time it sort of stings," added Lozowski, who had a youth trial with Premier League side Arsenal and played for Chelsea's academy before being released and focusing on rugby.

"I've played 198 games, could have got a couple more in there and had a little run and tried to make it to the top four?' That's what I was thinking at the time, but it doesn't always work out the way you want."

Lozowski, who starts in Sale's midfield alongside fellow summer signing Joe Marchant at Saracens on Sunday, admits proving his value to his old club, along with spurring on his new side's season, will be part of his motivation.

"I know Sale wanted me to come here and add value, which meant a lot to me," he said.

Lozowski is not the only member of Sale's travelling party who will be in familiar surroundings at the Stonex Stadium.

Director of rugby Alex Sanderson spent 17 years at Saracens, initially as a player before working as a coach at the club.

Brendan Venter, who has returned to Saracens this season and already been fined for opting out of media appearances, was Sanderson's first boss as a coach.

"I idolised Brendan to a degree," he said.

"A lot of his traits, his values and philosophies I'm aligned with. I've taken from them over the years.

"Not withstanding Mark McCall's unbelievable contribution [who led Saracens for 15 years between Venter's stints], it's good to have him back in the Prem as a character. I'm sure we'll see his character come out on to the field."

Sale are seeking to avenge two heavy defeats against Saracens last season, going down 65-14 away from home in October, before an 85-16 thrashing in April's reverse fixture.
